# The half-life of a recommendation {#sec-half-life}

Every recommendation in this book carries a date it does not print.

A strength label looks like a permanent property of a piece of advice. **Strong**
sits in a table next to *brush twice daily* and reads like a fact about brushing.
It is not. It is a fact about what a panel knew on a particular afternoon, and it
begins going out of date the moment it is set in type.

Usually that decay is slow enough not to matter. This chapter is about the cases
where it is not, and about the fact that one of them is sitting in the guideline
right now, at the end of a citation that points to a review which searches for
new evidence **every month**.

## How old is a national guideline?

The edition audited here was published on 10 September 2025. So a fair question,
and one nobody seems to ask of guidelines, is: how old was its evidence base on
the day it appeared?

Of the {{< var dboh.total >}} recommendations, {{< var dboh.dated >}} cite at
least one source carrying a publication year. For each of those I took the
**newest** year cited, because a recommendation is only as current as its most
recent support. The rest of the reference list can be as old as it likes.

| Age of the newest citation, at publication | Recommendations |
|:---|---:|
| Same year (2025) | {{< var dboh.age_same_year >}} |
| 5 years or older | {{< var dboh.age_5plus >}} of {{< var dboh.dated >}} |
| 10 years or older | {{< var dboh.age_10plus >}} of {{< var dboh.dated >}} |
| **Median** | **{{< var dboh.age_median >}} years** |
| Oldest | {{< var dboh.age_max >}} years |

: How current *Delivering Better Oral Health* was on the day it was published
{#tbl-citation-age}

The median recommendation in a guideline published in 2025 rested on evidence
most recently published in **{{< var dboh.age_median_year >}}**.

Two things make that number generous rather than harsh. A systematic review
published in 2013 closed its own literature search *before* 2013, so the evidence
underneath is older still than the citation year suggests; [Chapter
-@sec-varnish] traces one where the newest included trial was from 2012. And the
{{< var dboh.age_undated >}} recommendations citing nothing dated at all are
simply excluded here rather than counted as infinitely stale.

One detail is worth pulling out. The only recommendations whose newest citation
postdates 2023 are eight **Good practice** rows, and every one of them points at
another guidance document: the Scottish Dental Clinical Effectiveness Programme's
2024 periodontal guidance, or NICE's referral guidance as updated in July 2025.
The guideline's freshest citations are other guidelines. Its freshest research
citation is older than that.

## Old is not the same as decayed

I want to be careful here, because "the citation is twelve years old" is exactly
the kind of cheap point this book is supposed to be above. Age alone is not a
fault. There are three different situations and only one of them is anybody's
mistake.

**Settled.** The evidence is old because the question is answered and nobody is
still working on it. Running another trial would be waste. [Chapter -@sec-recall]
is the clearest case: the Cochrane review of recall intervals states that
"further studies comparing dental recall intervals for adults in primary care
seem unnecessary." A 2020 citation there will still be the right citation in
2035.

**Dormant.** The evidence is old because the trials stopped, not because the
question closed. [Chapter -@sec-varnish] is this: the varnish review's newest
included trial is from 2012 and its search closed in May 2013, not because
fluoride varnish is a solved problem but because nobody has funded the study.
That is a finding about the research economy, and [Chapter -@sec-research] is
about it. It is not a citation error. The guideline is citing the best thing
there is.

**Decayed.** The evidence moved, a newer version exists, and the guideline is
quoting the old one. This is the only one of the three that is a mistake, and it
is the only one a reader can neither detect nor forgive.

Two of these turned up in this book.

| Recommendation | Version cited | Newer version available | Available since |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `DBOH-084`, oral cancer adjunctive tests ([Chapter -@sec-cancer-screening]) | `CD010276.pub2`, 2015 | `CD010276.pub3` [@walsh2021] | July 2021 |
| `DBOH-074`, e-cigarettes ([Chapter -@sec-tobacco]) | `CD010216.pub3`, 2016 | `CD010216.pub9` [@lindson2025ec] | January 2025 |
| `DBOH-003` and three sibling rows, sugar ([Chapter -@sec-sugar]) | Moynihan and Kelly, 2014 | ten-year update [@moores2022] | March 2022 |

: Recommendations resting on a superseded version of their own cited review
{#tbl-decayed}

All three updates predate the September 2025 edition, the oral cancer one by more
than four years.

The sugar row is the one that shows the limits of automating this. The first two
are Cochrane reviews, which carry their version in the DOI, so a machine can spot
a superseded citation without reading a word. The sugar update is a separate paper
in a different journal with no version number attached to the thing it updates.
Nothing short of a real search finds it.

## The one that is hard to explain

[Chapter -@sec-tobacco] works through the e-cigarette row in detail, and I will
not repeat the whole of it. The short version is the part that belongs here.

DBOH tells its readers that its e-cigarette recommendation rests on "low
certainty evidence from one systematic review." That was a true description of
`CD010216.pub3` in 2016. By the time the guideline was published, the review had
been through seven further revisions and had reached **high certainty** that
nicotine e-cigarettes outperform nicotine replacement therapy
[@hartmannboyce2016ec; @lindson2025ec].

And the review had been announcing its own updates the entire time. Every version
since January 2024 says this in its published abstract [@lindson2024ec]:

> To ensure the review continues to provide up-to-date information to
> decision-makers, this review is a living systematic review. We run searches
> monthly, with the review updated when relevant new evidence becomes available.
>
> --- Lindson and colleagues, CD010216 [@lindson2024ec]

A **living systematic review** is one kept continuously current rather than
revised in occasional editions [@elliott2017living]. This one is maintained by
Cochrane with funding from Cancer Research UK, searches monthly, and publishes
under the same review identifier the guideline's own reference list prints. The
current version reports high-certainty benefit from 104 studies in 30,366
participants [@lindson2025eclive].

So the mechanism failed at the last possible step. Somebody had already done the
work of keeping this evidence current, had said so in the abstract, and had filed
it under the number DBOH was citing.

## I did the same thing, three times

This would be an easier chapter to write if the book were not guilty of it.

Four searches in this book failed, and they are recorded in
`appraisals/searches/` rather than quietly re-run. Three of the four are the same
failure as DBOH's:

- **[Chapter -@sec-amount]** searched for a Cochrane review by its identifier,
  got nothing useful back, concluded the 2010 version was current, and wrote in
  the chapter that the evidence "has not been systematically updated in fifteen
  years." A 2024 update existed [@wong2024].
- **[Chapter -@sec-cancer-screening]** searched the same way and missed the same
  review DBOH missed, `CD010276.pub3` [@walsh2021], published in 2021.
- **[Chapter -@sec-sugar]** searched on the 2014 review's authors and title, and
  missed its own ten-year update [@moores2022], which had upgraded the evidence
  for the 5% threshold a full level. DBOH missed it too.

The second and third are the useful ones. On both, the guideline and its auditor,
working independently and years apart, failed to find the same update by the same
method. That is not two instances of carelessness. That is one broken technique
used twice, and the lesson is written at the bottom of the search index:
**searching for a review by its identifier is not an update search.** An
identifier query finds the version you already know about. It cannot tell you
that a newer one exists, because you are asking it about the old one.

## What I would actually ask for

The temptation, having found this, is to propose running a living systematic
review for every recommendation. I do not think that is right, and it is worth
saying why, because it is the obvious conclusion and it is wrong.

Living reviews are for a specific situation, and the methods paper that named
them says which: they suit questions where "research evidence is emerging
rapidly, current evidence is uncertain, and new research may change policy or
practice decisions" [@elliott2017living]. All three, together. Most of this book
fails the third test and many chapters fail the first. Nothing new is coming for
tooth wear ([Chapter -@sec-wear]), and running a monthly search there would
produce a decade of confirmations that the trials still do not exist. Low
certainty is not a reason to search harder. It is usually a sign that nobody is
running the study.

Applied honestly to *Delivering Better Oral Health*, that rule admits very few
rows. Tobacco and e-cigarettes, where the literature is genuinely moving.
The oral cancer adjunctive tests, where the evidence has already separated in a
way the single Strong label does not reflect. Beyond those, the questions that
would repay continuous attention are mostly the ones outside the guideline
altogether, in [Chapter -@sec-fluoridation-works] and [Chapter
-@sec-fluoridation-harm].

So the proposal is not more reviews. It is three much cheaper things.

**Consume the living reviews that already exist.** DBOH did not need to build one
for e-cigarettes. Cochrane maintains it, Cancer Research UK pays for it, and it
searches monthly. What was missing was a subscription and somebody to read it.

**Print the version, not just the certainty.** Chapter 13 currently says "low
certainty evidence from one systematic review." Twelve extra characters would
have made this chapter unnecessary:

> Low certainty. `CD010216.pub3`, searched to January 2016.

A reader who saw that could check it in about forty seconds. A reader who sees
the sentence as written cannot check it at all, because the certainty is on one
page and the version is on another, and neither page says when the search closed.

**Say when the recommendation was last looked at.** Not when the guideline was
published; when each row was last checked against its own literature. A guideline
is not one document with one date. It is ninety-one claims with ninety-one dates,
and printing a single date on the cover conceals a spread of thirteen years.

::: {.callout-note title="What I searched, and when" collapse="true"}
PubMed, 20 August 2026, for the full version history of `CD010216`. Nineteen
records; I retrieved metadata for `.pub3` (2016), `.pub8` (2024), `.pub9`
(January 2025) and `.pub10` (November 2025) and read their structured abstracts.
Also PubMed for the living-systematic-review methods literature, from which
[@elliott2017living] is the defining paper.

The citation ages in @tbl-citation-age are computed, not counted by hand.
`scripts/extract_dboh.py` takes the newest publication year appearing in each
recommendation's reference list and subtracts it from 2025. The figures land in
`_variables.yml` and the table above reads them from there, so if the guideline is
reissued and the extractor re-run, this chapter's numbers move with it.

Two limits on that method, both of which make the table conservative. It reads
years off citation strings, so a review whose search closed years before it was
published counts as younger than its evidence really is. And the
{{< var dboh.age_undated >}} recommendations with no dated citation are excluded
rather than treated as maximally stale.

Full record in `appraisals/searches/ch32-half-life.md`.
:::

## What this means for you

Nothing about your teeth. This one is about how to read the advice rather than
what the advice is.

If you are ever told that something is backed by strong evidence, the useful
follow-up question is not "how strong?" It is **"as of when?"** The label does not
carry a date, and the gap between the label and its evidence is invisible from the
outside. In this guideline that gap runs to a median of seven years and a maximum
of thirteen.

And the same applies here. This book searched the literature in August 2026. On
the arithmetic in @tbl-citation-age, it will be about as current as *Delivering
Better Oral Health* was for roughly seven years, and then it will start being
wrong in ways I cannot predict from where I am sitting. Two of its chapters were
already wrong on this exact point before it was finished, and I only found out
because I looked twice.

The honest thing a book like this can offer is not permanence. It is a date, a
method, and enough working shown that you can tell when it has gone stale.
